title: Verifier‑Augmented vs. LLM‑Only NetOps Agents: A Paired Evaluation on an Action‑Aware Staging Benchmark
abstract: We report a fully preregistered paired evaluation that compared a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline on a compact action‑aware staging benchmark (ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1). The preregistered design (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1) used gpt-5-mini as the generator, deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as the runtime validator and post‑hoc scorer, N=400 paired tasks (800 episodes) and shared_initial_generation semantics (one shared LLM candidate per task). Confirmatory, artifact‑backed outcomes: complete_pairs = 400; baseline_success_count = 400/400; guarded_success_count = 400/400; paired contingency n_11 = 400, n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0; paired difference = 0.0; preregistered permutation p = 1.0; exact McNemar p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed=1729, 10,000 resamples); Cohen's h = 0.0. We emphasize up front that a preregistered design choice—shared_initial_generation together with reuse of deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as both runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer—produced a ceiling effect that made the primary estimand uninformative for this run. We preserve the full execution and analysis artifacts for reuse and describe how hardened follow‑on designs (independent per‑condition generation, adversarial injections, or heterogeneous validators) can expose verifier utility.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models are increasingly proposed for NetOps tasks that translate operator intent into device configurations and staged rollouts (canaries, progressive delivery, rollback). Prior prototypes and surveys document promise but also highlight a gap: action‑aware benchmarks that exercise end‑to‑end staged rollout semantics, blocking, repair, rollback, and provenance are scarce. Motivated by this gap we preregistered and executed a paired experiment (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1) to test whether adding a deterministic runtime validator to an LLM pipeline increases end‑to‑end safety (safe‑deploy rate) relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. The experiment used a paired design with N=400 deterministic intent→configuration tasks and two per‑task conditions: baseline (LLM‑only) and guarded (verifier‑augmented). Crucially, the preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics produced one shared LLM candidate per task that both conditions received; this isolates validator accept/block/repair behaviour on identical generator outputs. The research question was: Under a tightly controlled action‑aware staging benchmark, does a verifier‑augmented pipeline increase the paired safe‑deploy rate relative to an LLM‑only pipeline? Our principal contribution is an artifact‑backed, preregistered paired evaluation together with an evidence‑grounded failure analysis that explains why the selected design produced a null/ceiling outcome and provides concrete recommendations for benchmark hardening.
sections.related_work: Work on intent‑based NetOps, intent→configuration translation, and automated configuration generation has advanced rapidly (intent‑based NetOps, PreConfig, GraphSynth). Generate–validate–repair workflows and verifier‑guided IaC approaches report improvements in infrastructure contexts, suggesting verifiers can reduce configuration errors in constrained domains. Deterministic network verifiers and reachability tools have demonstrated the ability to detect configuration and policy violations offline. Simultaneously, agentic, tool‑augmented LLM architectures (ReAct, RAG, multi‑agent orchestrations) are applied to AIOps and NetOps but introduce new failure modes (hallucination, misapplied tools) that motivate runtime guardrails. Reviews and surveys call specifically for action‑aware benchmarks that measure rollout, blocking, repair, rollback, and provenance; our study operationalizes a compact staging benchmark under a strict preregistered design to probe these questions. The cited works underpin claims about prior capabilities and motivate the design choices summarized in our preregistration.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and primary estimand: The study preregistration (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1) specified a paired binary design with exactly N=400 deterministic tasks produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; primary test = permutation‑based paired test (two‑sided, α=0.05). Execution adapter and model: the adapter family was hosted_netops_gvr_v1 and the declared generator was gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json). Runtime validator and post‑hoc scorer were deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Shared_initial_generation semantics and model-call accounting: the preregistered shared_initial_generation setting produced one shared LLM generation per task that was delivered to both conditions; as a result model_calls_used = 400 (one shared generation per task) though planned episode_count = 800 (two condition episodes per pair). This design intentionally isolates validator accept/block/repair behavior on identical generator outputs rather than testing generator variance. Deterministic consistency and exclusions: deterministic three‑replay consistency checks were preregistered; exclusions were defined for nondeterministic runs, simulator/internal errors, or provenance duplication. The execution manifest shows completed_episode_count = 800, completed_pairs = 400, failed_episode_count = 0. Repair policy: adapter allowed up to one repair call per task (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1); in this run repair_applied = false across episodes. Analysis plan and exact procedures: the preregistration specified the permutation‑based paired test as primary confirmatory analysis and corroborating exact McNemar two‑sided check; bootstrap CIs for median time‑to‑rollback and paired difference were specified as secondary/descriptive metrics. All analysis steps, seeds, and resampling counts (bootstrap_seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000) were recorded and archived.

sections.discussion: Primary interpretive conclusion: the observed null/ceiling outcome is a predictable consequence of two preregistered design choices, not evidence that runtime verification is broadly unnecessary. First, shared_initial_generation produced identical generator outputs for baseline and guarded conditions, removing generation variance as a mechanism for the guarded adapter to change outcomes. Second, the runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer were the same deterministic implementation (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) so acceptance decisions and post‑hoc scoring were necessarily concordant. Construct validity consequence: because the same validator accepted the identical shared candidates and also scored outcomes, the experiment measured validator acceptance on identical candidates rather than independent closed‑loop generator+guard dynamics. Statistical and power implications: the preregistered power rationale assumed non‑ceiling baseline rates and intra‑pair variability; the observed ceiling invalidates that rationale for this run (the permutation test and McNemar check correctly reflect the observed identical outcomes). Practical recommendations for benchmark hardening (artifact‑grounded): (1) remove shared_initial_generation to allow independent per‑condition generation and expose generator‑level failures; (2) introduce targeted adversarial or perturbation seeds that produce invalid candidate generations for at least a fraction of tasks; (3) evaluate heterogeneous generator and validator pairings so the runtime guard and scorer are not identical; (4) include explicit rollback/repair decision utilities in the adapter so repairs, when invoked, produce measurable divergence in outcomes. These recommendations are consistent with evidence and gaps identified in the literature synthesis and can be operationalized starting from the archived artifacts (execution/task_manifest.jsonl and execution/responses/*). Reproducibility and artifact summary: the key archived analysis artifacts referenced in manuscript figures/tables are analysis/results.json, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/paired_difference_figure.svg, analysis/analysis_log.jsonl and the execution manifest execution/execution_manifest.json; full execution traces, validator traces, and per‑task manifests are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl and execution/raw_results.jsonl in the artifact bundle.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline and an LLM‑only pipeline on a compact action‑aware staging benchmark. Under the preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the particular generator+validator pairing, every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5; both conditions produced 100% safe‑deploy on N=400 pairs and the preregistered permutation test returned p = 1.0. This ceiling outcome stems from preregistered design choices (shared candidate semantics and reuse of the deterministic validator as guard and scorer) that removed opportunities for the guard to alter deployments. We therefore do not claim general evidence about the utility of runtime verification in heterogeneous deployments. We release the preregistration and full execution/analysis artifacts so researchers can reproduce the run and use the artifacts as seeds for hardened experiments that exercise blocking and repair behaviors.

limitations: Benchmark hardness and ceiling effect: under preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator, every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 so the guard had no opportunity to alter outcomes; this makes the primary estimand effectively untestable in this run and invalidates the original power rationale.

Model and scope: experiment used a single generator (gpt-5-mini) and a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); results do not generalize across models, validators, or production heterogeneity.

Construct validity: the same deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementation served as both runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer; this conflation produces concordant acceptance/scoring and limits inference about independent closed‑loop verifier utility.

Shared candidate semantics: preregistered shared_initial_generation (one LLM generation per task shared by both conditions) intentionally reduces generation variance and therefore limits inference to the validator’s behavior on identical candidates rather than full generator+guard closed‑loop interactions.

Synthetic environment and external validity: the simulator and validator do not fully model production telemetry noise, operator workflows, or adversarial actor behaviours; external validity to live networks is limited.
Adversarial robustness untested: adversarial or distribution‑shifted prompts and generator faults that could trigger guard interventions were not exercised in this run and remain open.

Aggregated difficulty reporting gap: the full per‑task difficulty labels are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl; an aggregated histogram by difficulty level for all N=400 tasks was not summarized in the top‑level manuscript artifacts and therefore remains a preserved reporting limitation (readers can derive the complete aggregation from execution/task_manifest.jsonl in the archived bundle).
